extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, IP litigators, judges, and applicants working on diagnostic/biomedical patents
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria for determining whether patent claims (particularly diagnostic/medical method claims) recite patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, with emphasis on claims that implicate laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature / natural phenomena / abstract ideas not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas’ are not patentable subject matter under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an implicit exception to §101 recognized in Diamond v. Diehr, Benson, Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, etc. Examples: a newly discovered mineral, E=mc^2, or Newton’s law are not patentable. Use this as the baseline exclusion when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must do more than state the law and add 'apply it'
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite the natural law and tell a practitioner to apply it (e.g., 'measure X and apply correlation Y') are insufficient. See Benson, Parker v. Flook, and the Court’s repeated admonition that 'apply it' alone does not create eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / additional elements required
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process that focuses upon the use of a natural law must also contain other elements or a combination of elements (sometimes referred to as an 'inventive concept') sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the natural law itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether additional claim features provide practical assurance the claim is an inventive application (e.g., Diehr’s integrated steps added significance). Mere identification of audience, recital of the law, or conventional measurement steps do not constitute the requisite inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely conventional or obvious pre-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely conventional or obvious pre-solution activity previously engaged in by researchers is normally not sufficient to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed steps (apart from the law itself) are well-understood, routine, conventional, or 'insignificant post-solution activity' (e.g., standard measuring techniques, telling a practitioner to do what they already do), they do not make the claim patent-eligible. See Flook and Mayo’s analysis of the 'determining' step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition cannot be circumvented by limiting technological environment or adding insignificant activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition against patenting abstract ideas or laws of nature cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment or by adding insignificant post-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely confine the law to a particular setting (e.g., doctors treating patients) or append trivial steps are still subject to exclusion. Quoted: prohibition 'cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment.' (Bilski/Diehr)

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is a useful clue, not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is an important and useful clue to patentability but is not the definitive test of §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim involves a transformation (e.g., administering a drug, analyzing blood) or a machine, eligibility still requires that the claim not effectively be a claim to a law of nature. Transformations that are routine or that could be performed by future non-transformative techniques may not satisfy §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / tying-up-future-innovation concern
rubrics_metrics.description: A central concern is that patent claims should not improperly tie up the use of laws of nature and thereby inhibit future discovery and innovation; claims that effectively monopolize basic tools are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim would foreclose others from making further refinements or combining the law with later discoveries. Historical examples include Morse and Benson; Mayo holds that claims telling doctors to measure and consider correlations risk tying up subsequent treatment decisions and future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claimed steps as a whole and separately; additive significance required
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether additional steps, individually and as an ordered combination, add something significantly more than the natural law itself; a new combination can be patentable only if it contributes more than conventional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr permitted patentability where the additional steps integrated the equation into a process in a nonconventional way. By contrast, Mayo finds that where each step is conventional and the combination adds nothing beyond the sum of parts, §101 exclusion remains. Ask: are the steps unconventional and do they meaningfully integrate the law?

rubrics_metrics.name: Administering / determining / wherein claim elements can be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements of the type 'administering' (identifying intended audience), 'determining' (measuring by any process), and 'wherein' (reciting the correlations) may be insufficient where they merely: identify users, recite the natural law, and instruct routine measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo’s claims reciting these three steps were invalid because (1) administering only picked out an audience, (2) wherein clauses merely informed the audience of the natural laws, and (3) determining instructed routine conventional measurement 'through whatever process the doctor wishes to use.' Such step-types should be scrutinized for conventionality and preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making patent eligibility depend on draftsman's art
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility must not be allowed to 'depend simply on the draftsman’s art'—courts must look to underlying principles rather than claim phrasing alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentability turns solely on how the claim is drafted (e.g., clever wording to recite an application of a law), §101 analysis should identify whether the substance is an attempt to monopolize a law of nature despite form.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 inquiry is distinct from §§102/103/112; cannot be displaced
rubrics_metrics.description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is a separate gatekeeping inquiry and cannot be displaced or made redundant by novelty (§102), obviousness (§103), or written description/enabling (§112) analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying exclusively on later sections to police claims that are essentially to laws of nature would render the §101 exception meaningless. Courts should apply §101 first to prevent claims that would otherwise preempt foundational scientific tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will not parse narrowness of laws of nature as a substitute for exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Even narrow or specific laws of nature can inhibit future research; precedent does not distinguish patentability by narrowness of the law—courts rely on a bright-line exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume narrow scope means patentable; Mayo declines to distinguish among laws of nature based on narrowness because courts are ill-suited to make fine-grained judgments about downstream innovation impacts.
